finding: Round 2's §2.4 removal inventory named `securityHeadLineCap` and the `headLines` helper alongside `selectSecurity`; the round-3 rewrite dropped both from the list while still deleting their only reader. `headLines` (internal/engine/auditfiles.go:197-198) and `securityHeadLineCap` (:19-20) are referenced from exactly one place — selectSecurity's content branch at :166 — which §2.4 item 3 removes when it drops the content half of the heuristic. `.golangci.yml` enables `unused`, which reports unreferenced unexported constants and functions, so an implementer following §2.4's enumerated consequences literally ships two orphaned symbols and fails the `golangci-lint run` half of the quality gate. This is the same defect the round-2 finding about `roleSecurity`/`roleMaintainability` closed in §2.1, reintroduced in the section that was rewritten.

resolved.evidence: Confirmed: securityHeadLineCap and headLines are read only from selectSecurity's content branch, and .golangci.yml enables `unused`, so leaving them would fail the quality gate. §2.4 item 3 now names both as removed with the content half, and item 2 states containsSecuritySubstring is renamed matchesPriorityPath so the surviving predicate stops naming a filter that no longer exists.

suggestion: Add `securityHeadLineCap` and `headLines` to §2.4 item 3 as removed with the content half, and state that `containsSecuritySubstring` survives as the path-ranking predicate, so the inventory again names every symbol the change orphans and leaves none for the `unused` linter.

finding: §1 is byte-identical to round 2 except for the schema clause, so its diagnosis still reads 'the behavior depends on a role id string and an English keyword list, neither of which is part of the role contract tp documents', and its closing paragraph still promises only that the release 'removes the id-based dispatch and neutralizes the language-specific default auditor prompts'. §2.4 reversed the round-2 decision: the keyword list is not deleted, it survives as `priorityPathSubstrings` and now orders the file list of EVERY role instead of one. Half the defect §1 diagnoses — undocumented English keyword behavior — is therefore kept and widened, and the Overview never says so; a reader of §1 alone concludes the list is gone, and nothing in §1 or §4 records that it now governs every role's file selection.

resolved.evidence: §1's closing paragraph now carries the reversal: the keyword list is explicitly excluded from what the release removes, described as demoted from a per-id filter that could empty a role to a ranking signal applied identically to every role, with the condemned magic narrowed to the id dispatch and the list's power to drop a role.

suggestion: Reconcile §1 with §2.4: state in the closing paragraph that the keyword list survives as a ranking signal applied uniformly to every role (and is documented as such), and reword the empirical-properties sentence so the surviving list is presented as a retained, documented mechanism rather than part of the condemned magic.

finding: §2.4 item 3 presents its removal list as complete ("the field, its assignment, and the function are all removed"), and §2.1 is equally careful to delete the now-unread roleSecurity/roleMaintainability constants — but deleting selectSecurity also orphans two symbols the spec never names: securityHeadLineCap (internal/engine/auditfiles.go:20) and headLines (auditfiles.go:198). Both are read only from inside selectSecurity's HeadReader branch. .golangci.yml enables the `unused` linter, so leaving them in place fails `golangci-lint run` — the mandated quality gate at tp done. Separately, containsSecuritySubstring survives unrenamed while its only data source is renamed to priorityPathSubstrings, reproducing in miniature the misleading-name trap §2.5 exists to remove.

resolved.evidence: Same orphaned symbols as the regression lens's incomplete-removal-inventory finding, fixed together in §2.4 item 3 (securityHeadLineCap, headLines) — and this finding's second half drove the containsSecuritySubstring → matchesPriorityPath rename now stated in item 2, so the predicate and its input share one honest name.

suggestion: Extend §2.4 item 3's removal list to securityHeadLineCap and headLines (both unreferenced once selectSecurity is gone, and both flagged by the enabled `unused` linter), and state in item 2 that containsSecuritySubstring is renamed alongside its list (e.g. matchesPriorityPath) so the ranking predicate and its input share one name.

finding: §2.5 gives `SpecCoverageTotal` a two-branch definition — "the task-mapped set in the normal branch, and the filtered universe in the no-task fallback branch" — and that is the subtlest new claim in §2, since the two pools differ exactly when a task file maps only part of the diff. No §7 item observes it. Item 10's only spec-coverage assertion is that "a `spec-coverage` prompt renders `max 20`", which is §2.6's non-truncated form and is satisfied by any total less than or equal to the list length; its `10 of 34` case is a code-file role. An implementation that sets `SpecCoverageTotal` to the filtered universe size in both branches (or to the list length always) passes every listed test while rendering a wrong count in exactly the case the count exists to report.

resolved.evidence: §7 item 17 added, pinning SpecCoverageTotal on both branches: a task file mapping fewer files than the diff with a task-mapped set exceeding AuditFileCap must render '## Affected Files (20 of <task-mapped size>)', and a spec with no task file must total the filtered universe. The finding's own argument is recorded in the item — without both cases an implementation that always uses the filtered universe passes.

suggestion: Add a §7 item that, on a spec whose task file maps fewer files than the diff touches and where the task-mapped set exceeds `AuditFileCap`, asserts the `spec-coverage` header renders `## Affected Files (20 of <task-mapped size>, max 20)` — and a second case with no task file asserting the total equals the filtered universe size. Both are needed to distinguish the two branches.

finding: Two round-2 findings on §2.8's miscounting preamble were resolved by dropping the arithmetic claim ('Three committed tests encode the behavior being removed ... and one must be widened') in favour of a named exhaustive search. The round-3 revision reintroduces an arithmetic claim — 'Six committed tests are affected:' — followed by seven numbered items, and those items name at least nine test functions (item 3 names TestFilterFiles_Security and TestFilterFiles_Cap20; item 5's mechanical rename covers TestFilterFiles_Maintainability and TestFilterFiles_DropFirstBackfill). The count is wrong under every reading, in the one section whose value is its claim to be exhaustive.

resolved.evidence: The arithmetic claim is gone for good. §2.8's preamble now says the list itself is the contract and carries no count, with the reason stated inline (a count is one more thing that can drift out of step with the list) so a later revision does not reintroduce a third one.

suggestion: Delete the numeral from the preamble — e.g. 'The inventory below is exhaustive against a search for every committed reference to ... Each committed test it touches is listed:' — so the enumerated list is the sole contract and no count can drift out of sync with it again.

finding: §2.8's header contradicts its own list twice. (a) It says "Six committed tests are affected", but items 1-7 name seven distinct tests (EmptyRoleOmitted, RouteChecklist_Disjoint, FilterFiles_Security, FilterFiles_Cap20, DropsBinaryFixturesDeleted, BodyOrderAndEmbedding, CLAUDEmdOnlyForMaintainability), and item 5's unnamed references live in two further tests — TestFilterFiles_Maintainability (auditfiles_test.go:99) and TestFilterFiles_DropFirstBackfill (auditfiles_test.go:130) — for nine in total. (b) The exhaustiveness claim rests on a search for sel.Security, selectSecurity, HeadReader, roleSecurity, roleMaintainability, '## Project Context', and '## Affected Files (max 20)' — a set that cannot surface `sel.Maintainability`, `selectMaintainability`, or `MaintainabilityFileCap` (the identifiers §2.5 renames, and precisely what item 5 itself lists). The stated evidence does not support the stated guarantee for the release's widest-reaching change.

resolved.evidence: §2.8's preamble drops the count, and the searched-literals list gained sel.Maintainability, selectMaintainability, MaintainabilityFileCap, securityHeadLineCap, headLines, containsSecuritySubstring and the JSON role keys. TestFilterFiles_Maintainability and TestFilterFiles_DropFirstBackfill are now named explicitly in item 5, with the note that their fixtures carry no priority keyword so the §2.4 ranking leaves their alphabetical expectations valid.

suggestion: Add Maintainability / MaintainabilityFileCap / selectMaintainability to the searched-literals list, name TestFilterFiles_Maintainability and TestFilterFiles_DropFirstBackfill explicitly under item 5 (noting their fixtures contain no priority keyword, so the §2.4 ranking leaves their alphabetical assertions valid), and correct the count to match the enumeration.

finding: §2.9 is the fixture definition §7 item 2 depends on, and two of its terms are not reachable as written. (a) "Both roles are then the inliner" is not guaranteed by the fixture it describes. The fixture is "a corpus whose only non-`spec-coverage` role is the one under test", i.e. `spec-coverage` is present, and emission order is fixed with `spec-coverage` first (asserted today at internal/cli/audit_named_test.go:33-35). The `inlinerDone` latch goes to the first emitted role whose file set fits, so `spec-coverage` takes it and neither role under test is the inliner — unless the fixture spec is authored with no structured elements so `spec-coverage` is skipped, which §2.9 and §7 item 2 never say. Two engineers build materially different corpora and specs from this description. (b) "byte-identical after replacing the role id string and the output path" does not say what the output path is replaced with, or why it differs at all once the ids are equal-length and substituted — leaving the normalization step, and therefore the assertion, unwritten.

resolved.evidence: §2.9 is now a three-clause fixture with each clause's reason stated. The spec-coverage problem this finding identified is clause 2: spec-coverage is dropped from the fixture corpus entirely, because emission order puts it first and it would take the inlinerDone latch. The normalization is also made concrete — substitute the role id token and rewrite the output path audit-r<N>-<role-id>.ndjson.

suggestion: State the fixture completely: whether `spec-coverage` is present and, if so, that the fixture spec carries no structured elements so it is skipped and the role under test is first (or drop `spec-coverage` from the corpus entirely). Replace "and the output path" with the concrete normalization (e.g. "after substituting the role id and rewriting each invocation's temp-dir prefix to a fixed token"), so both engineers write the same comparison.

finding: §2.9's equal-length-id rule is necessary but not sufficient for the byte-identity comparison it prescribes. fileCheckItems builds the slug from `<path> Apply the <role-id> role rules to <path>` and truncates at 40 chars (audit_roles.go:96-97, slugifySubject:138). Equal-length ids guarantee the same cut position, but when the cut lands inside the id occurrence the prescribed normalization — "replacing the role id string" — cannot map one prompt onto the other, because only a prefix of the id survives. Concretely, for a 23-char path such as internal/cli/audit_x.go the slug ends ...apply-the-securi vs ...apply-the-sekuri; the example pair `security`/`sekurity` diverges at index 3, so the two prompts differ and §7 item 2 fails even though no id branch survives. Any fixture path of length 22-28 hits this.

resolved.evidence: Clause 3 of the new §2.9 answers this directly: equal length alone is insufficient because the 40-character slug truncation can bisect the id occurrence, so the fixture requires ids differing only in their final character (security/securitz), which makes every truncated prefix identical and holds the comparison for any path length.

suggestion: Constrain the fixture so the truncation can never bisect the id: either pick the pair so the ids differ only in their final character (e.g. `security`/`securitz`, making every truncated prefix identical), or state a path-length bound that keeps the id wholly inside or wholly outside the 40-char window, and say the normalization is a whole-token replace of the id.

finding: §2.2 was rewritten this round to emit the disposition rule as a new `## Disposition` block placed immediately after `## Checklist` in every shared-arm prompt — a change to the prompt body structure that tp documents. skills/tp/REFERENCE.md:400 states that structure verbatim ('Role -> Role Rules -> Spec Excerpt -> Project Context -> JSON-array Checklist -> Affected Files -> Output Schema') and becomes wrong the moment §2.2 lands. §4 was rewritten in the same revision but requires the four documents to record only the routing rule and the changed embedded defaults, and §7 item 14's guard asserts only those substrings, so no task owns the fix. Round 2 had no such gap because the disposition wording lived inside `expected_evidence`, which no document describes.

resolved.evidence: §4 now requires REFERENCE.md's and SKILL.md's prompt-body-order line to be rewritten, giving both new orders explicitly: the shared-arm order with the ## Disposition block and Project Context, and the spec-coverage order with Spec Excerpt and neither.

suggestion: Extend §4 to require REFERENCE.md's prompt-body-order row to carry the `## Disposition` block for shared-arm prompts (and, while there, the §2.6 affected-files header forms), so the documented prompt contract matches the emitted one.

finding: §4 enumerates exactly what the four documents must say (the reserved-id routing rule, the file-<role-id>-<slug> item-id form, the changed default prompts) and §7 item 14 guards it by substring, but two of the four already document the audit prompt's body order verbatim — skills/tp/REFERENCE.md:400 and skills/tp/SKILL.md:309 both state 'Role → Role Rules → Spec Excerpt → Project Context → JSON-array Checklist → Affected Files → Output Schema'. §2.2 inserts a new '## Disposition' block into that order for every shared-arm prompt and §2.3 changes who receives '## Project Context', so both lines become stale and neither §4 nor its guard notices. §4's own standard is that the four docs 'must all tell one story'.

resolved.evidence: Same doc drift as the regression lens's doc-contract-gap finding, fixed together in §4 — and this finding's identification of SKILL.md:309 alongside REFERENCE.md:400 is why both files are named. While verifying it, a third staleness surfaced and is now also covered: both documents state prompts[].role as an enum of the three built-in ids, wrong since user-defined roles shipped in v0.25.0.

suggestion: Add the prompt body order to §4's required updates: REFERENCE.md and SKILL.md must show the '## Disposition' block in the audit prompt order and state that '## Project Context' now goes to every non-spec-coverage role (with '## Spec Excerpt' spec-coverage-only), so no document keeps a body order the release invalidates.

finding: §4 states two documentation requirements at very different levels of pinning. The first paragraph pins exact substrings (`spec-coverage is the only reserved auditor id`, and the forbidden `file-sec-`/`file-maint-`) and §7 item 14 asserts them mechanically. The second paragraph — "All four must also record that the embedded default auditor prompts changed in this release and that an already-ejected corpus keeps its old copies" — pins no substring and no §7 item asserts it, so it is not a testable requirement: two engineers write four different sentences and neither can fail a check. This is the requirement §5 item 3 explicitly leans on ("The §4 documentation notice is how a user learns the shipped defaults moved"), so the load-bearing half of §4 is the untestable half.

resolved.evidence: §4's second requirement is now pinned like the first: each of the four documents must contain the substring 'ejected role files are not rewritten on upgrade', and §7 item 14 asserts it alongside the reserved-id substring.

suggestion: Pin a substring for the second requirement the same way as the first (e.g. every one of the four docs must contain `ejected role files are not rewritten on upgrade`), and extend §7 item 14 to assert it alongside the existing substring — or state explicitly that this paragraph is a prose-review obligation with no automated guard, so no one expects a test to catch its absence.

finding: §6's second paragraph enumerates the upward deltas as exactly two (§2.3's up-to-50 conventions lines, §2.6's header count) and concludes 'Net prompt size for such a role is roughly unchanged'. Two problems. (a) §2.2's '## Disposition' paragraph is a third upward delta — a ~5-line fixed block added to every shared-arm prompt, i.e. every prompt except spec-coverage — and it is absent from the accounting even though §2.2 was itself restructured on cost grounds. (b) The conclusion does not survive the arithmetic §6 itself presents: minus up-to-10 affected-file lines against plus up-to-50 conventions lines, plus ~5 disposition lines, plus a header count, is roughly +45 lines per prompt, not 'roughly unchanged'. The single case where 'roughly unchanged' (or better) genuinely holds is the one role holding the §2.9 inliner latch, whose 10 dropped files also drop their inlined contents — but §6 never draws that distinction, so it states the claim for every already-emitting role while it holds for at most one role per invocation.

resolved.evidence: §6's second paragraph rewritten as explicit arithmetic: three upward deltas (§2.3 up to 50 lines, §2.2 the ~5-line Disposition block, §2.6 a few header characters) against one downward (up to 10 fewer path lines as the cap falls from 20 to 10), giving roughly +45 lines for a paths-only role. The 'roughly unchanged' conclusion is gone, with the note that it did not survive its own arithmetic, and what the growth buys is stated in round-trips rather than lines.

suggestion: Enumerate three upward deltas (§2.3 up to 50 lines, §2.2 ~5 lines once per shared-arm prompt, §2.6 a few characters) against the one downward delta (up to 10 path lines), and replace 'roughly unchanged' with the direction those numbers actually give: a paths-only role's prompt grows by up to ~45 lines, while the one role that holds the §2.9 inliner latch shrinks by the contents of the files it no longer inlines. Keeping the §2.2 block off the ledger is the specific gap; the release does not need the net to be zero, only stated.

finding: §7 item 8 pins the `## Disposition` paragraph only positively and only by count: "Every shared-arm prompt contains the `## Disposition` paragraph exactly once". §2.2 makes two further claims that no §7 item asserts. (a) The negative half — §2.2 scopes the paragraph to "every shared-arm prompt", so `spec-coverage`'s prompt must not carry it (the sentence "A file containing nothing in this role's domain is a PASS" is nonsense over table-row/list-item/finding items), yet nothing asserts its absence there. An implementation that writes the paragraph unconditionally in `buildRolePrompt` — the simpler implementation — passes every listed test while contradicting §2.2. Compare §7 item 9, which pins both directions for `## Project Context`. (b) The placement half — §2.2 pins "immediately after the `## Checklist` block", and item 8 claims to be "pinning §2.2's once-per-prompt placement", but a count assertion is satisfied by a paragraph emitted anywhere in the body. No test pins block order for a shared-arm prompt at all: the only body-order test, `TestAuditPrompts_BodyOrderAndEmbedding`, indexes solely the `spec-coverage` prompt (audit_prompts_test.go:28-44).

resolved.evidence: §7 item 8 now carries three assertions — exactly once in every shared-arm prompt, absent from the spec-coverage prompt, and positioned between ## Checklist and ## Affected Files ( — and §2.2 gained a paragraph stating the spec-coverage exclusion and its reason (the disposition sentence is meaningless over table-row and finding items), so the negative half is specified as well as asserted.

suggestion: Extend item 8 to three assertions: the paragraph appears exactly once in every non-`spec-coverage` prompt; it does not appear in the `spec-coverage` prompt; and its index is greater than the index of `## Checklist` and less than the index of `## Affected Files (` in each shared-arm prompt. State the spec-coverage exclusion explicitly in §2.2 rather than leaving it implied by "shared-arm".

finding: §2.4 item 3 enumerates the symbols the content-heuristic removal takes with it (`AuditFileInputs.HeadReader`, its assignment, `GitHeadReader`) but omits the two symbols that `selectSecurity` is the sole consumer of: `headLines` (the helper) and `securityHeadLineCap` (the 200-line constant). Once `selectSecurity` is deleted both are unreferenced, and `unused` is an enabled linter in `.golangci.yml`, so `golangci-lint run` — the quality gate — fails until they are deleted too. Because the spec is precise elsewhere about which now-dead symbols go (§2.1 names `roleSecurity`/`roleMaintainability` explicitly), the omission reads as an instruction to keep them. The same item also leaves `containsSecuritySubstring` unaddressed: it survives as the ranking predicate but keeps a name pointing at the list §2.4 item 2 renames to `priorityPathSubstrings`.

resolved.evidence: Same orphaned symbols as the high-severity finding of this round, fixed together in §2.4 item 3, including the containsSecuritySubstring rename this finding also proposed.

suggestion: Extend §2.4 item 3's removal list to `headLines` and `securityHeadLineCap` (both orphaned by the deletion of `selectSecurity`), and state in item 2 that the predicate helper is renamed alongside its input (e.g. `containsSecuritySubstring` -> `matchesPriorityPath`) so no symbol keeps the old security-filter naming.

finding: In the truncated header form '## Affected Files (10 of 34, max 10)' the first number and the cap are provably always identical. The list is the first CodeFileCap (or AuditFileCap for spec-coverage) entries of the ranked order, and this form is rendered only when the pre-cap total exceeds the list length — which can only happen once the cap has bitten, at which point the list length is exactly the cap. 'max 10' therefore restates the leading '10' in every prompt rendering this form, and feeds no decision the auditor makes: 'of 34' already carries the whole truncation signal. (The 'max N' of the non-truncated form is earned — an item count below the cap is how an auditor infers nothing was dropped.)

resolved.evidence: Correct — the truncated form renders only once the cap has bitten, at which point the list length is the cap, so 'max 10' provably restates the leading '10'. §2.6's second form is now '## Affected Files (10 of 34)' with that reasoning stated inline, and §7 item 10 updated. Both forms still satisfy the '## Affected Files (' prefix match §2.8 item 6 relies on.

suggestion: Render the truncated form as '## Affected Files (10 of 34)' and keep '## Affected Files (max 10)' for the complete case; both still satisfy the '## Affected Files (' prefix match that §2.8 item 6 and §7 item 10 rely on, and §7 item 10's expectations shorten accordingly. If the repeated cap is kept on purpose (e.g. so both forms name the cap uniformly for a reader who sees only one prompt), state that in §2.6 so the repetition reads as a decision rather than an oversight.

finding: Item 6 says `TestAuditPrompts_BodyOrderAndEmbedding` "breaks twice", the first breakage being that "it locates the affected-files block by the literal `## Affected Files (max 20)`, which §2.6 rewrites". §2.6 does not rewrite that literal for this fixture: the lookup at internal/cli/audit_prompts_test.go:33 is against the `spec-coverage` prompt, whose cap is 20, and the fixture supplies exactly one affected file (`--affected-files auth_helper.go`), so the pre-cap total (1) equals the list length (1) and §2.6's first form renders `## Affected Files (max 20)` verbatim. The test breaks once — on `assert.NotContains(t, sec, "## Project Context")` at line 65. A stated breakage that does not occur is a claim an implementer will act on and a reviewer will fail to reproduce, in a section whose only job is inventory accuracy.

resolved.evidence: Correct on both counts. §2.8 item 6 now states one breakage (the ## Project Context assertion), explains why the header lookup does NOT break (a single affected file to a spec-coverage prompt makes the pre-cap total equal the list length, so §2.6 renders that exact string), and presents the prefix-match change as deliberate hardening rather than a required fix.

suggestion: Rewrite item 6 as a single breakage (the `## Project Context` assertion for `security`) and present the prefix-match change to `## Affected Files (` as a hardening against future §2.6 truncation rather than as a required fix — or change the fixture to two-plus affected files so the truncation form actually applies and the stated double breakage becomes true.

finding: The lead-in says "Six committed tests are affected:" and is followed by a seven-item list that names more than seven distinct tests: `TestGenerateAuditPrompts_EmptyRoleOmitted`, `TestRouteChecklist_Disjoint`, `TestFilterFiles_Security`, `TestFilterFiles_Cap20`, `TestFilterFiles_DropsBinaryFixturesDeleted`, `TestAuditPrompts_BodyOrderAndEmbedding`, `TestGenerateAuditPrompts_CLAUDEmdOnlyForMaintainability`, plus the two tests item 5 covers without naming (`TestFilterFiles_Maintainability` and `TestFilterFiles_DropFirstBackfill`, verified in internal/engine/auditfiles_test.go:99-146) — nine. Since §2.8's whole value is its exhaustiveness claim, a stated count that no reading of the list produces undermines the one property the section asserts, and gives a reviewer no fixed number to check completion against.

resolved.evidence: Same count mismatch as the two other §2.8 findings, fixed together: the numeral is gone and item 5's two tests are named, so every entry is checkable by name.

suggestion: Either correct the count to match the list and name item 5's two tests explicitly (making every entry checkable by name), or drop the numeric claim and say "The inventory below is exhaustive against that search; each entry names the tests it covers."

finding: §2.8 item 6 asserts TestAuditPrompts_BodyOrderAndEmbedding 'breaks twice', the first breakage being its lookup of the literal '## Affected Files (max 20)'. Under §2.6 that literal is still rendered exactly when the pre-cap total is at most the list length, and that test's spec-coverage prompt has a single affected file (auth_helper.go via --affected-files, no task-mapped commits), so its header stays byte-identical and the lookup at audit_prompts_test.go:33 does not break. Only the NotContains(sec, '## Project Context') assertion actually fails. The inventory that claims exhaustiveness overstates one of its own entries.

resolved.evidence: Same misattribution as the tester's test-breakage-misdiagnosis finding, fixed together in §2.8 item 6 — the inventory no longer overstates the breakage, which matters precisely because the section claims exhaustiveness.

suggestion: Restate item 6 as one real breakage (the '## Project Context' assertion) and keep the prefix-match on '## Affected Files (' as a deliberate hardening against the count form, not as a required fix — or change the fixture so the truncated form is actually exercised there.

finding: §2.8's framing claim does not match its own list. It says "Six committed tests are affected", but the seven numbered entries name seven distinct test functions (item 3 alone names both `TestFilterFiles_Security` and `TestFilterFiles_Cap20`), and item 5's "remaining `sel.Maintainability` and `MaintainabilityFileCap` references" sweep additionally covers `TestFilterFiles_Maintainability` and `TestFilterFiles_DropFirstBackfill` in the same file — nine committed test functions in total. An implementer using the stated count as a checksum against a compile failure stops short. The exhaustiveness justification is also weaker than stated: the named symbol search (`sel.Security`, `selectSecurity`, `HeadReader`, `roleSecurity`, `roleMaintainability`, `## Project Context`, `## Affected Files (max 20)`) cannot see the CLI-level tests keyed on the role-name string, which is where items 1, 2 and 7 actually live, and it misses `TestAudit_FileFilterCap` (`internal/cli/integration_test.go`), whose `security` assertion "affected_files capped at 20" survives compilation but stops constraining anything once that role is bounded by `CodeFileCap` = 10.

resolved.evidence: TestAudit_FileFilterCap is now §2.8 item 7: it supplies 50 path-matching files and asserts the security prompt's bound, which becomes CodeFileCap, so the assertion is retargeted rather than deleted — noted as the only committed test exercising the cap end-to-end. The searched-literals list also gained the JSON role keys this finding proposed.

suggestion: Correct the count (or drop it and let the list stand), add `internal/cli/integration_test.go`'s `TestAudit_FileFilterCap` as an entry — its `security` bound becomes 10, so the assertion should be retargeted or folded into §7 item 7's literal-cap test — and state the search set as `byRole["security"]` / `byRole["maintainability-conventions"]` plus the symbol list, since the role-name string is how the CLI-level tests reach the changed behavior.

finding: §7 item 7 asserts the cap literals explicitly ("`CodeFileCap` is asserted as the literal 10 while `AuditFileCap` is asserted as the literal 20, so a silent cap change fails a test"), but the release's other pinned constant gets no such guard: §2.4 item 2 requires `priorityPathSubstrings` to keep "the same five values `lock`, `validate`, `auth`, `secret`, `perm`", and no §7 item asserts the set. Items 4 and 5 exercise ranking through a single keyword, so dropping four of the five values, or adding a sixth, changes which files any role reads first and fails nothing. Given that the rename from `securitySubstrings` is a touch of that very declaration, a silent edit is the plausible failure.

resolved.evidence: §7 item 16 added, asserting priorityPathSubstrings equals exactly [lock, validate, auth, secret, perm] with this finding's rationale recorded: the rename from filter to ranking signal is exactly when a value is most likely to be quietly dropped, and items 4 and 5 exercise only one keyword each.

suggestion: Extend item 7 (or add an item alongside item 4) asserting `priorityPathSubstrings` equals exactly `["lock", "validate", "auth", "secret", "perm"]`, mirroring the cap-literal guard and its stated rationale.
